Good afternoon, Excellencies, distinguished participants. I declare open the 5th meeting of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Human Rights of Older Persons. This afternoon we will resume our plenary discussions under item 4. Señoras y señores distinguidos—

Ladies and gentlemen, Dear colleagues, Excellencies, and friends, as we begin this segment, it is my pleasure to present to you the document. I would like to be clear from the very start: this document is not a draft treaty. It is not expecting any results nor is it trying to predefine any particular format or architecture. Quite simply, it is an invitation to begin. It has been drafted bearing in mind the contributions of States as well as the comments that have been made during this process and the views of national institutions, experts, and civil society. It seeks to identify amid legitimate differences, possible starting points for discussion. Because if one day we do want to have a legally binding instrument, then we must begin by asking ourselves how we're going to change our expectations into rights. How are we going to give greater clarity to the principles, to have more specificity in the obligations, and to make the whole Consistent. We're not starting with a blank page. There is a vast corpus of international human rights law, and our task is to see if we can build upon it, to add to it wherever necessary, and to address the protection gaps that we have heard of so frequently in this room. And we must recall an essential point. Any instrument that ends up coming out of this process will not be written alone. It will be the result of a convergence of wills. It must cross borders, legal systems, and different traditions. It must be understood by governments and presented to the constitutional processes of nearly 200 countries. That is the sheer size of the task before us. But it is also the vast size of our responsibility. Which is why this document is not closing any doors. Indeed, it is opening them all up. It does not present conclusions. Rather, it raises questions. It doesn't tell us what our endpoint shall be. It simply tells us, or suggests to us, a starting point for our common travels. The document you have before you now can change, be transformed, can be fit into, or even significantly reworded. And that is honestly what we expect from this debate. And it is in that spirit of openness that I invite you to share your observations, your criticisms, and proposals. The document is open for discussion. The debate has been launched, and now all of you have the floor. Thank you.

Excellencies, colleagues, delegates coming from capitals, representatives of the national human rights institutions, of civil society entities, of organizations of older persons. Ladies and gentlemen, today is a historic day. Up until yesterday, most of the discussions On the recognition of the human rights of older persons gravitated around why we should have a legally binding instrument at all. As of today, the discussions turn around what this instrument should be. In this framework, the Chair has decided to propose the inclusion of a 3-hour segment into the work program on our assessment of any and all issues that might garner a consensus. And so, in light of that, last week we distributed a document that has an introduction, a suggested structure for a treaty, and regulatory principles. And so, the introduction includes a reminder of the adoption of Resolution 58/13 of the Human Rights Council, in virtue of which we find ourselves here today. And we point out the importance of recognizing the demographic trends of the 21st century. Characterized by aging, by low birth rates, and by the challenges faced by the social security systems. In the preamble of the treaty, we say that some of the issues to be addressed shall be the human dignity of older persons and equality before the law. Democratic transition, of which we spoke just a moment ago, how important it is to include in the process every stakeholder, recognizing that older persons are not a homogenous group. And additionally, in the general provisions, principles and scope of application, We suggest that we should avoid a rigid definition of older persons and that we postpone the discussion to the national level and that we define principles such as equality before the law and non-discrimination on the grounds of age. From the practice of other international instruments, we see that a legally binding instrument Ought to bring in other principles as well, such as freedom, the right to development of their own personhood, duties and responsibilities of the community, privacy, the inclusive participation anchored on equal opportunities, equality and non-discrimination, with an express prohibition of discrimination on the grounds of age, And recognizing the interdependence to find a balance between resilience and family support. Additionally, we identified some cross-cutting topics, among them recognizing national and cultural diversity, the family support systems, and community support systems in keeping with applicable law. Among the substantive rights, we believe that the very core of the instrument ought to include an approach of equal opportunities, a positive translation of state obligations into rights and obligations for older persons, Full equality before independent, impartial courts and tribunals in keeping with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and other treaties. Freedom from abuse, negligence. The right to health. The right to private property and a decent life. long-term care, digital inclusion, and the opportunities that come from the right of education. All of these provisions stand to be clarified as appropriate, subject to national legislation in the framework of what is available for the obligations of a state In keeping with different contexts and national possibilities, including accessibility and the availability of quality services. Regarding the implementation, we note very strong support to the contributions that have been received. To a robust implementation mechanism and establishing a committee with periodic obligations to report. The participation of the older persons themselves in any activities regarding the future treaty can be clarified among member states In order to arrive at a standard of international law that would emerge from these negotiations. In addition, the future treaty, in our view, should have ratification clauses, clauses of entry into force and amendments, in line with the Vienna Convention on the Right— the Laws of Treaties. And recognize that any topics that are not directly addressed in the final provisional section ought to be considered in light of the Convention, as for example withdrawal following a 1-year notification timeframe. Among the regulatory principles that we believe could assist in guiding its effective implementation We have that a rights-based approach on aging can be useful in recognizing, of course, the paradigm shift of charity and welfare to one of rights, the freedom and the right to development and the personhood of old persons. We also believe that the instrument ought to strike a balance between supporting decision-making and the respect for the will and preferences of the person. Also, we believe that care, as a human right, and redefined as a several-stakeholder responsibility that is not just limited to the family and doesn't ignore it, Is an area in which regulation, financing, and oversight is needed, as well as the prevention of abuse and negligence. Now, that would include setting quality standards, as well as a code of conduct for geriatric institutions, as well as the recognition of the course of life perspective, given that inequalities accrue throughout time with the concomitant need to develop preventive policies, which is also addressed. And lastly, to recognize that older persons are not a homogeneous group. The instrument can address as well discrimination against women, Persons with disabilities, rural life, persons under institutionalized care, as well as people requiring support. It is our hope that this document will contribute to guide our deliberations and can be used as one of the foundations to continue to build together a robust and broadly shared instrument that would lead to a consensus. Thank you, Mr. Chair, Rapporteur. First of all, Malta aligns with the EU statement to be delivered shortly. Malta thanks you and the Secretariat for making the Food for Thought paper available for consideration by delegations as the process of elaborating a legally binding instrument commences. The Food for Thought paper is in our view a first early draft proposal for this Intergovernmental Working Group's work. In the Preambular Section, it is noticeable that the well-established concept of the enjoyment of human rights, an inherent right to all, is missing. The LBI should establish ab initio not just dignity and equality, but reaffirm older persons' enjoyment of human rights in toto. An additional issue of concern, also applicable throughout the paper, is the introduced concept of duties. In our assessment, the formulation listed in the preamble part of the paper does not accurately reflect Article 29 of the UDHR and seeks to expand the principle beyond its current normative understanding. We express our cautious approach on this point, noting in this LBI— that in this LBI should be drafted to imply that the well-established principle of persons being the rights holders and the duty— and that the duty is on the state to promote, protect, and defend implementation of all human rights is modified or reversed. Certainly, this process should not be a vehicle for reinterpretation of any longstanding norms and principles. This position applies for such references in Section 1, Preamble, Roman II principles, Roman III cross-cutting issues, Section 3 substantive rights, Roman 4, subsection 2, a human rights-based approach to aging. Moving on to the definition section, we would like to ask for clarification on the source of language for the term right to development of their own personality. We would consider it useful if the eventual legally binding instrument would utilize language which has already been well established in an effort to not create confusion of terms. Also with other definitions which are unrelated to older persons. We would thus suggest changing every reference to dignity and the free development of their personality in line with Article 22 of the UDHR. This applies to Section 4, Subsection 1, entitled A Human Rights-Based Approach to Aging. In Section 3, Substantive Rights, we seek a clarification on what the 3rd bullet means. Since it is referring to independent and impartial tribunals, and then lists the UDHR as an example. We are not aware that there are any tribunals or similar structures associated with the UDHR. Under Section 3, Care as a Human Rights Issue, Malta expresses its caution on proposals which seem to imply developing a code of conduct. We do not believe that this is the role of function of the eventual LBI. Additionally, Malta believes that this elaboration process should limit itself to its mandate and not attempt to include other elements which may seem valid but do fall outside the scope of the legally binding instrument, such as the notion in the same section of support to informal caregivers. Our understanding is that such items are handled under national employment law and standards. Only a few more sentences left. In Section 5, entitled Discrimination, we also seek clarification on what basis was this listing formulated and whether contributions from states and civil society were consulted in its compilation. As always, creating lists inherently carries the risk of exclusion. In this sense, we ask why gender-diverse persons are not included in this section, or in the paper as a whole? Gender-diverse persons, as we know, also become older persons and thus would enjoy the provisions of any future legally binding instruments. Furthermore, was consideration given to include in this listing indigenous and minority groups? This is by no means presented as a definitive list on our part, but an indicative one. As part of this process, the Intergovernmental Working Group should develop a legally binding instrument that is inclusive and one that also caters for possibly marginalized groups. Having presented Malta's initial reaction to the Food for Thought paper, we also suggest that the paper should be further enhanced beyond the generic approach, which is often limited in its scope. An LBI should take into account current issues and trends and not limit itself to the traditional aspects of the rights of older persons. We propose in this regard that older persons' right to make their own choices is clearly introduced and not just limited to the aforementioned personality development, and it should also delve deeper into issues of active participation in all aspects of civil and political rights, in enjoyment of all civil, cultural, economic, and social rights as the right holders. Digital inclusion, as already mentioned briefly in the paper, should be further strengthened as this concept will be highly important for older persons as more services become more online-oriented. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, Rapporteur. Austria aligns its statement as well with the statement to be delivered by the EU later on, and we would like to thank for preparing the food for thought paper on guiding principles and structure. The future convention will require further discussion, this is clear, refinement as well, as well as supplementation. It will be important to ensure that its structure reflects the lived realities of older persons in all their diversity and across different regions, social contexts, and life situations. Austria agrees that the future instrument should follow a clear and coherent structure. It should include a preamble, general principles, definitions, or a provision of scope, substantive rights, implementation and monitoring provisions, and a final clause. We would also see merit in considering a section on general obligations of States, Such a section could provide guidance on the types of measures States may take to support implementation of the Convention, including legislative, administrative, policy and awareness-raising measures, taking into account different national contexts and capacities. For Austria, the instrument must be firmly rights-based. It should respond not merely to demographic ageing, but to structural barriers, ageism and discrimination that prevent older persons from enjoying their human rights on an equal basis with others. In this regard, we believe that ageism should be explicitly addressed. Ageism is not only a matter of individual attitudes. It is a structural factor that can lead to exclusion, unequal treatment, violence, lack of access to services, and the denial of autonomy and participation. The convention should build on and not weaken existing human rights standards. This is particularly important in relation to gender equality, disability rights, legal capacity, autonomy, independent living, community inclusion, and protection against multiple and intersectional discrimination. Austria also supports a flexible, functional rights-based understanding of older age. The approach developed by the 2014 Council of Europe recommendation may provide useful inspiration. At the same time, the definition should remain adaptable, allowing it to respond to evolving societal realities and potential changes in the global context, while remaining consistent with the object and purpose of the instrument. On care and support, Austria recognizes their importance for the effective enjoyment of human rights of older age. However, the precise legal framing of obligations in this area requires further discussions, taking into account national systems, competences, and responsibilities. We would suggest focusing on human rights-compliant, accessible, affordable, and quality-assured care and support systems, including oversight, accountability, support for informal carers, and decent working conditions for care workers. Finally, Austria would like to highlight social isolation and loneliness as important cross-cutting challenges. They should be addressed through social inclusion, participation, accessible services, and community-based support. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Demographic realities like life expectancy and national legal frameworks differ considerably across countries. Accordingly, some degree of flexibility to reflect national realities and contexts is both appropriate and necessary. Mr. Chair, Nigeria particularly welcomes the emphasis placed on respect for national and cultural diversity. Community and family support systems, and intergenerational solidarity as guiding principles. More importantly, we welcome the balanced approach reflected in the paper, which recognizes not only the rights of older persons but also the important role of families, communities, and intergenerational solidarity in promoting their dignity and well-being. As reflected in our general system— general statement, in many societies, particularly in Africa, families remain the first source of care and support for our older peoples. We therefore consider it important that any future instrument should recognize and strengthen that role while complementing rather than replacing the primary responsibility of states. With regard to substantive rights proposed, we appreciate that the paper seeks to build on existing international human rights law while responding to the realities associated with aging. As our discussions progress, it will be important to ensure that the future instrument complements existing human rights treaties and remains practical and implementable across different national contexts. Nigeria also believes that greater prominence should be given to the economic rights and economic empowerment of older persons. Thank you very much. Thank you, Chair Rapporteur. Thank you.

The recognition that older persons are not a homogeneous group, the intersection between disability and age, the importance of addressing the gap between rural and urban areas. First, it is important to begin from the premise that older persons rights holders, and that states are the primary duty bearers responsible for respecting, protecting, and fulfilling their rights. Secondly, we must start from the understanding that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated, as well as the principle of progressive realization of human rights. While we must bear in mind the importance of diverse national and cultural contexts, It is the state's duty to promote and protect all human rights, regardless of their political, economic, and cultural system, as established by the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action. Third, it is essential to highlight the importance of the autonomy of older persons, the respect and protection of their legal personhood, as well as the right to independent life and inclusion in the community. These are core topics. Fourth, we believe that it is important for references to care and support systems to be aligned with the terminology, definition, and concepts that were adopted already in various international bodies, including the Human Rights Council, the General Assembly, the ILO, as well as by agencies such as UN Women and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. In this regard, it must be recognized that older persons may require care and support, but that often, in many cases, it is they who provide care for family members, Particularly older women. Care is shared responsibility in families, communities, and private sector, and the state. And so in this context, ensuring access to care and support systems is primarily an obligation of states, so that the enjoyment of rights does not depend on capacities of family members. Care work, whether paid or unpaid, has been recognized as work within the framework of the ILO. While those receiving care and support must never be seen as a burden or obstacle, it is important to recognize that care responsibilities fall disproportionately on women, particularly older women, and this compromises their own care needs and their own enjoyment of their rights.

We are open to consider proposals from other delegations on the structure of the instrument, including the possibility of adding yet other sections in addition to the one we have proposed. Let me begin by expressing our sincere appreciation to Argentina for preparing and sharing this paper. We commend your leadership and your commitment to the process during your chairmanship. Allow me to highlight 7 points. First, we consider that the text lacks balance in relation to the responsibility for supporting older persons with an excessive emphasis on responsibilities of family members. While Brazil fully recognizes the essential role played by families in supporting and caring for older persons, we also believe that there must be a balance among the complementary responsibilities of families, societies, and states. In addition, we would suggest referring to families in the plural to reflect the diversity of families arrangement. Second, Brazil is essential to recognize that older persons may— oh, sorry— persons, especially women, persons with disabilities, persons of different sexual orientations, migrants, persons living in poverty, traditional peoples, and persons who belong to the ethnic racial, national, linguistic, religious, and rural groups. IRDs may experience multiple intersecting forms of discrimination, which often create additional vulnerabilities and affect the full enjoyment of their human rights and fundamental freedoms. Third, we attach particular importance to a gender perspective. Older persons frequently experience multiple intersecting forms of discrimination resulting from persistent gender inequalities and remain disproportionately exposed to physical, psychological, and other forms of violence. This should also be recognized. Fourth, we would welcome explicit reference to combating ageism alongside all forms of violence against older persons, addressing age-based prejudices and stereotypes for them to ensure the true realization to their lives, their rights. Brazil considers autonomy to be a central concept that should be reflected through the document. Promoting the autonomy, independence, social integration, and effective participation of older persons should remain one of the guiding objectives of the future instrument. Thank you, Chair. First of all, we thank the Chair-Rapporteur for the organization of this session. We appreciate the efforts to facilitate a constructive discussion on the possible contours of a future legally binding instrument. However, Belgium will only be in a position to express its views on a possible future legally binding instrument once a draft text has been presented. However, allow me to share some preliminary views from our side. For Belgium, the core principles of the future LBI should be firmly grounded in the recognition that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated. References to national context or cultural specificities should not be used in a manner that could weaken universally agreed human rights standards. It is, however, critical to foster local ownership. Regional organizations have played an essential role in bringing universal norms closer to local realities, including on the human rights rights of older persons and can serve as a source of inspiration in addition to existing human rights treaties. We welcome the vision that the overarching framework of the future legally binding instrument should be fully consistent with existing human rights treaties. In this regard, it is essential to reaffirm that states are the primary duty bearers for the respect, protection, and fulfillment of human rights, while older persons should be fully recognized as right holders. Ensuring their agency, dignity, and individual autonomy is fundamental to the effective enjoyment of these rights and to their full and meaningful participation in decisions that impact their life. With regards to the role of families, families have long been at the heart of most societies. However, societies continue to evolve, and families today take different forms. Any future legally binding instrument should reflect this diversity. At the same time, it should recognize individual family members as right holders in their own right and ensure that the rights of older persons who do not belong to any family structure are equally respected, protected, and fulfilled. In that regard, it is critical to acknowledge that while families play an important role in care and support systems, a disproportionate share of paid and unpaid care work continues to be undertaken by women and girls, and and which that constitutes a primary driver of gender inequality. We welcome the reference to non-discrimination, as prohibition of discrimination remains one of the most fundamental principles of international human rights law and is a key principle to ensure the human rights of older persons who may experience multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination throughout their lives. Any future treaty should therefore reflect an intersectional approach, recognizing that older persons may face multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination on various grounds, including gender, ethnic origin, age, disability, religion, socioeconomic status, political opinion, and other characteristics. Such an approach is essential to ensure the full enjoyment of the human rights of older persons. I thank you.

We offer the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. We would like to thank the Chair for the Food for Thought paper and welcome this opportunity to offer some preliminary reflections, though we will, of course, need to consider proposals in greater detail, and we reserve the right to refine our views as discussions evolve. First, it is clear that older people are already rights holders. The UK is committed to protecting their rights. In considering the development of any future instrument, it is important to recognize that many of the rights relevant to older persons already exist within the international human rights framework. Rights contained in instruments such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights already apply to older persons as they do to all individuals. To the greatest extent possible, we should avoid duplicating, recreating, and weakening existing norms, and instead build upon the well-established human rights framework that already exists. Relatedly, we note that a number of the principles reflected in the paper are already addressed in existing human rights treaties, whether in the core treaties or in the more specialized instruments. For example, issues relating to access to a fair hearing and due process are addressed in the ICCPR, while protection against exploitation, violence, abuse, and neglect are reflected in instruments such as the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. In our view, these existing standards provide a logical starting point for this discussion. Second, we believe it is important to remain clear about the nature of human rights obligations. Human rights establish legal obligations on States in relation to individuals, as has been echoed by some several delegations before us. Accordingly, our focus should be on elaborating and clarifying those obligations. While families, communities, and other social actors undoubtedly play an important role in supporting older persons, they are not themselves bearers of international human rights obligations in the same way that states are. Third, we would underline the universal nature of human rights, as has also been echoed by several other delegations. While states may adopt different approaches to implementation in light of their own legal systems and circumstances, the content of human rights is universal and applies equally to all individuals. Human rights obligations are not contingent on national, cultural, or regional particularities. Finally, on a specific point, we would welcome further clarification regarding the proposal that older persons should enjoy a right to develop their own personality. We would be grateful to hear more about the intended scope and legal basis of this concept and how it relates to existing rights recognized under international human rights law. I thank you.

Thank you, Chair Rapporteur. Many thanks also for preparing the Food for Thought paper, which we see as a first basis for the discussion today. It is indeed important to move to more concrete conversations. The panel yesterday and all the submissions helpfully summarized this morning also feed this discussion and help us to take into account the experience, input, and lived realities of older persons, as well as inputs from around the world. As mentioned in our general statement, within the EU, we still need to deliberate more in detail on our common position on the elements of a future instrument. At the same time, we would like to contribute to this discussion with a couple of further initial comments. Our general statement underlined that the development of standards relating to the rights of older persons must be based on and fully aligned with international human rights law, including the CRPD, as well as regional instruments. A few points to make this more concrete. Any further instrument on human rights of older persons must embody and adhere to the principles of universality, indivisibility, interdependence, and interrelatedness of human rights. This was also underlined by many speakers today. Firmly rooted in the UDHR, the principle of universality asserts that rights apply to everyone globally regardless of culture, geography, or status. This was also confirmed in the VDPA. Secondly, any future instrument must be fully and firmly human rights-based. It must, as I already said, build on and strengthen existing standards. This should be fully reflected in the preamble of a future instrument and permeate the whole text. Thirdly, international human rights law is founded on the principle that every person possesses inherent dignity and equal rights. Therefore, the older persons must be recognized as individual rights holders and states as duty bearers. Fourthly, if international human rights law addresses duties, if individuals hold specific responsibilities, they are carefully articulated and primarily concern the duty not to violate the human rights of others. Fifthly, as mentioned in previous EU statements, We need to advance the full enjoyment of human rights by older persons without discrimination. This requires the future instrument to fully incorporate principles of non-discrimination, equality, and autonomy, while recognizing the diversity of older persons and taking a life course approach, and explicitly address ageism, age-based stereotypes and prejudice, age-based discrimination. Multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination require specific attention, as does the protection of those those who are in a disadvantaged, vulnerable, and marginalized situations. Sixth, the future instrument should also provide clear guidance on the prevention and protection from all forms of violence, abuse, neglect, and exploitation, and should ensure access to justice. Seventh, we support further discussion on a flexible approach regarding the definition of older persons, taking into account different national contexts while ensuring effective protection. Eighth, the future instrument should promote the meaningful and effective participation of older persons in all decisions. Ninth, the future structure should be clear and coherent and include the regular elements of a human rights treaty. And then, for— leave me to leave a 10th point. The future instrument should be one that enables the practical translation into concrete improvement of the enjoyment of human rights by older persons. And the pros and cons of including concrete implementation measures as guidance should be discussed within this working group. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, rapporteur. The Czech Republic aligns with the EU statement. The Czech Republic thanks the authors of the Food for Thought paper for their contribution to the discussion of the possible architecture and guiding principles of a legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons. Once again, our starting point is that, as in the CRPD, Age should never constitute a barrier in access to human rights and freedoms. In our view, older persons are active rights holders, not merely passive recipients of care or subjects to the decisions of others. We welcome the paper's emphasis on dignity, equality, non-discrimination, autonomy, participation, protection from violence and neglect, and access to care and support. At the same time, We believe that the future instrument should have clear added value in relation to existing international human rights treaties. It should identify and address age-specific protection gaps, including age-based discrimination, autonomy and supported decision-making, prevention of abuse and neglect, long-term care, the situation of older persons in institutional and other dependent settings, digital inclusion, and access to justice. The Czech Republic supports a flexible, context-specific— excuse me, context-sensitive understanding of older person, avoiding a rigid age threshold while ensuring sufficient legal clarity and consistency in implementation. We suggest, for example, a set maximum age limit, for example 65, like in the CRC, which can be lowered by the state parties. While family, community, and intergenerational solidarity are important, they should not be formulated in a way that shifts the primary responsibility for respecting, protecting, and fulfilling human rights away from the state. References to available resources may guide the progressive realization of social rights, as it is the case in the ICESCR, but must not weaken immediate obligations such as non-discrimination, protection from violence, and neglect, access to justice, and respect for autonomy. The Czech Republic supports a flexible and context-sensitive approach to implementation. However, references to national, cultural, or social diversity should not be understood as allowing limitations on universal human rights or as justifying discrimination, violence, neglect, or restrictions, restrictions on autonomy. As regards the possible treaty body, The future instrument could draw inspiration from the CRPD committee model, in particular Article 34 of the CRPD, which requires due consideration of the participation of experts with disabilities in the committee's composition. By analogy, the future treaty body on the rights of older persons should ensure the meaningful participation of older persons with relevant expertise among its members. Finally, We attach great importance to the meaningful participation of all the persons and their representative organizations throughout the process in line with Human Rights Council Resolution 58/13. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, rapporteur, for giving me the floor. Germany aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Thank you for the food for thought paper inspiring debate. Human rights are individual rights which are fully applicable at all ages, so a comprehensive non-discrimination clause, including addressing multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination, must be a central part of the new LBI. International human rights law is founded on the principle that every person possesses inherent dignity and equal rights. Therefore, older persons must be recognized as individual rights holders and States as duty bearers. At this early stage, we would like to make the following methodological observations. As already stated in our input to the 3 guiding questions, we are in favor of pursuing the structure of preamble recalling and reaffirming existing standards, treaties, and norms, which are fully applicable to all ages, and thus setting the scenery. Scope: what is the group of older persons? As we have heard Monday and yesterday, there's a broad consensus on the substance stance, building on the results of the 14 sessions of the Open-Ended Working Group on Aging and the areas of concern identified and consented in the form of recommendations in Decision 14/1 of the Open-Ended Working Group, bearing in mind the regional instruments, and last but not least, the MIPAP process. Regarding the follow-up, we think the specificities should be discussed when a broad consensus is reached on the substantial clauses of the Convention. Chair.

Turkey welcomes the Chair's Food for Thought paper and appreciates the effort to provide a structured basis for the discussions. We would like to present several observations. With regard to the proposed preamble, Turkey supports emphasizing the inherent dignity and equal rights of older persons, as well as recognizing demographic aging as one of the defining global trends of our time. However, we would encourage language that reflects both the opportunities and the challenges associated with longevity, avoiding an approach that presents aging primarily as a policy burden. Turkey also welcomes the recognition that older persons are not a homogeneous group and that diversity among older persons should be reflected throughout the LBI, such as older women and older persons with disabilities. Regarding the guiding principles, Turkey welcomes the recognition of important role played by families and communities. Nevertheless, we believe that the instrument should clearly maintain the distinction between the supportive role of families and the legal obligations of States under international human rights law. The primary responsibility to respect, protect, and fulfill human rights should remain with States. Türkiye would favor maintaining flexibility regarding the definition of older persons. A rigid chronological threshold may not adequately reflect differing demographic realities and national contexts. Turkey also believes that certain concepts appearing throughout the paper could benefit from further refinement. In particular, terminology relating to autonomy, independence, legal capacity, and supported decision-making may provide greater legal certainty than broader references to the development of one's personality. Regarding substantive rights, we would like to draw attention to social security and economic security of older persons, and also encourage the use of well-established terminology drawn from existing international human rights treaties wherever possible. For instance, Turkey would favor replacing the expression decent living with the established term adequate standard of living, as this would ensure greater consistency with existing treaty language, particularly the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Finally, Türkiye considers that any future monitoring mechanism should complement the existing United Nations treaty body system, avoid unnecessary institutional duplication, and promote dialogue, technical cooperation, and capacity building. I thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Chair Rapporteur. Uruguay wishes to express its appreciation for the preparation of this discussion paper. Which we regard as a basis for a structured discussion on the architecture and the guiding principles of a future instrument. We appreciate the proposed structure, including the preamble, the general provisions, substantive rights, which we believe must be strengthened, as well as the implementation mechanisms and the final clauses. We also share the recognition that international human rights law does not adequately address the specific challenges faced by older persons. We also welcome the references to equality, non-discrimination, participation, autonomy, long-term care and digital inclusion, and a life cycle approach. However, as we see it, certain aspects need to be strengthened. At first, we would like to present the following comments. To begin, we believe that it is important for the future treaty to better reflect that its primary goal is to establish binding obligations for States, that references to national legislation, available resources, and different national contexts should not weaken the universal nature of the rights recognized therein, nor the responsibility of States to respect, protect, and guarantee those rights. Second, we encourage to offer greater precision in several key areas such as mental health, rehabilitation, accessibility in all its dimensions, social protection, adequate income, palliative care, protection from institutionalization, abuse and neglect, as well as effective access to justice and appropriate remedies. Third, we consider it essential to strengthen an intersectional approach One that recognizes that older persons may face multiple types of discrimination, including on the grounds of gender, disability, ethnic or racial origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, Indigenous status, migration status, or socioeconomic situation. Regarding the role of the family, Uruguay recognizes that families and communities play a fundamental role in providing support, accompaniment, and care for many older persons. Human Rights Watch welcomes the recognition in the Food for Thought paper of equality and non-discrimination, dignity and autonomy. Human Rights Watch is, however, concerned that the paper frames the treaty as a response to aging. Aging is a natural part of life and is not itself a driver of human rights violations. Instead, the treaty should recognize and respond to ageism and other drivers of rights violations against older persons. Human Rights Watch is also concerned by the emphasis on care institutions and the characterization of older persons as dependent. This is inconsistent with the principles of the UN Convention on the Rights of persons with disabilities. The Disability Rights Convention recognizes persons with disabilities, including older persons with disabilities, as full autonomous rights holders who actively contribute to the development of society and have the right to support systems tailored to their needs that empower independent living. A treaty that characterizes older persons as dependent risks reinforcing negative ageist attitudes and stigmatizing older persons further. Human Rights Watch is also concerned that references to family and community duties and responsibilities for older persons could be interpreted as diminishing states' human rights obligations. Families and communities have an important role to play, and states should support them in doing so. However, as an international human rights instrument, The treaty should articulate and reinforce states' obligations to respect, protect, and fulfill the rights of older persons, rather than be underpinned by an assumption that responsibility rests with families or communities. Human Rights Watch agrees with the Chair that the treaty should avoid a rigid definition of an older person. However, allowing each state to determine who falls within the treaty's scope would undermine its universality. Instead, the treaty should articulate to whom it applies in line with its purpose of ensuring the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by older persons. Third, the LBI should not include provisions that permit exceptions, limitations, or restrictions that reduce the level of protection of human rights guaranteed under other human rights treaties. It should also ensure that no existing limitations, exceptions, or biases in law and practice that have constrained the full and equal enjoyment of human rights by older persons are carried forward or replicated in its provisions. It must instead remedy gaps and overcome the current conceptual limitations that have historically limited the full and equal realization of human rights in old age. While chronological age may provide administrative clarity, reliance on age thresholds can embed assumptions and stereotypes about older persons and also may fail to account for the diversity of ageing experiences. The drafting process should therefore carefully examine the tension between age-based classifications, the prohibition on age discrimination, and the obligation to achieve substantive equality through recognition of intersectionality. In our view, the Convention should develop dynamic, inclusive, and adaptable definitions that avoid rigid age-based limitations and ensure the instrument remains responsive and future-proof. To do otherwise would be antithetical to our role here today. Finally, the paper makes no explicit mention of this issue of intersectionality, and we consider this to be an omission. As the Chair's paper helpfully recognises, there needs to be a sharp move away from the current charity and welfare model to recognition that older persons should have the same rights and freedoms and the same respect for legal capacity as anyone else. The key to achieving this will be a complete shift from all forms of institutionalisation to creative community-based options rooted in the will and preferences of older people in all their diversity. It will be essential that however extensive some older person's support needs may be, it is older persons, not professionals, family members, friends, or others, who choose what services older people receive and in what form, but older people's decision, aided by supported decision-making, when they would value it. In addition, this fundamental change of approach replaces the assumption that it's adequate just to improve current services and that some older persons will always have to be institutionalised regardless of their wishes and experience certain restrictions to their autonomy. The UNCRPD deinstitutionalisation guidelines provide some useful examples of rights-based, community-based forms of support, for example, personal assistance, peer support networks, circles of support, user-led centres for independent living, and assistance from family members and friends all grounded in respect for older persons' own choices and the lifestyle which is important to any one individual. For older persons who prefer to live in communal settings, co-housing settings run by their members are one creative option, including cross-generational forms of these. For older persons experiencing crisis, Crisis houses which provide support for them based on their own choices are an important resource. When older persons need intensive support, the key element to rights-based communal living will be services which are controlled by residents and attuned to both individual and group wishes. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. While demographic trends are undeniable, we respectfully suggest that the first core message needs to be reversed. We should not start speaking of a challenge, but rejoice is that human beings live longer, thanks to life and medical advances. So our task is to promote older persons' enjoyment of human rights across the world, living in societies that strive to secure access for all to quality lives, including through better socioeconomic rights. Ageism needs, therefore, to be specifically addressed. Since the raison d'être of a new specific convention is to define the States' responsibility to uphold the human rights obligation, this must be stated in the preamble. Individuals, families, in whatever form they are shaped across the world, and communities have certainly a key role to play, but we cannot shift responsibility, not substitute for the role of the States. It is good to speak about supporting intergenerational solidarity, But language about family duties does not fit a legal binding instrument, as we cannot pass responsibilities to families and communities, especially to older women, as mentioned in the debate, for lack of policies or inadequate funding. On care, we cannot only discuss long-term care or informal care. Healthy aging and care have to be addressed, including through access to free quality public services and through extending decent work to those who provide care for older persons. Quality life should be ensured at home until whenever possible, or creating alternative living arrangements that would respect free choices and dignity, as my friend just said. As per Social Security policies and in line with ILO Convention 102 and Recommendation 202, the instruments need to indicate commitment to paths to social protection for all. While countries are certainly free to adapt national policy at local level and in discussion with national stakeholders, the instruments need clear guidelines, a robust framework, and adequate follow-up at international and national level to be credible and We look forward to a successful exercise. Thank you, Chair. The IHPC thanks you for explicitly including palliative care as part of the right to health in the Food for Thought paper. A rights-based approach to palliative care will require public health services to relieve the severe pain and burdensome symptoms experienced by older persons with serious illness through interdisciplinary patient-centered practices. The WHO estimates that only 14% of people with palliative care needs receive it globally, mostly in high-income countries. Stipulating palliative care as part of the right to health in an LBI will go a long way to remedying that egregious inequity that penalizes those most in need, particularly in the Global South. We align with the Global Alliance for the Rights of Older Persons joint position paper in insisting the LBI explicitly prohibit age discrimination. Ageism is a scourge in public and private health systems worldwide that often prevents older persons from accessing palliative care services that support their self-determination and freedom of choice, including around end-of-life decision-making, distribution of property, place of death, disposition of remains, and other key legal matters. Explicit prohibition of age-based discrimination in healthcare, including in hospice and palliative care systems where they exist, is essential to protect dignity, the right to health, and the right to be free from torture. The Global Healthy and Compassionate Communities Movement, recently celebrated at the WHO conference in Spain, showcased the governance support for age-friendly communities anchored in mayoral and city council offices. This global movement testifies to the principle of subsidiarity and state support for communities that are willing to step into the widening breach left by health and social systems as regards aging, serious illness, and bereavement. A legally binding instrument that recognizes palliative care will protect older persons at the most vulnerable time of their lives. It will uphold standards for ambulatory and home-based care to protect the resilience of households and survivors, shepherding through the trauma of serious illness, and bereavement.

The Center for International Environmental Law welcomes the framework outlined in the Chair's Food for Thought paper to guide the architecture of the legally binding instrument. As this working group considers the underlying principles general obligations and specific rights of the new legally binding instrument, we must ensure it is fit for the realities of the 21st century. To achieve this, we would urge states to integrate a holistic twofold approach to the environment. On one hand, the legally binding instrument should explicitly identify the triple planetary crisis— climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution— as a structural threat to older persons. And on the other, it should formally enshrine the autonomous right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment. Numerous human rights mechanisms and institutions have made clear that older persons are rights holders whose specific needs must be addressed and whose meaningful participation must be ensured in climate and environmental decision-making, disaster risk reduction, and policy design at all levels. They have called on states to adopt age-inclusive, disability-inclusive, and gender-responsive climate laws and policies that recognize older persons' rights, resilience, and agency. The right to a healthy environment has already been recognized by the UN General Assembly and the Human Rights Council, as well as regional mechanisms. Including this right among those protected under the legally binding instrument, it would thus be essential to ensure that the instrument is consistent with international human rights law. Therefore, in alignment with the proposed structure of the instrument, we urge member states to embed environmental rights into the text across 2 levels: substantive obligations explicitly requiring states to protect older persons from environmental disruption affecting their rights and include the right healthy environment among the protected ones. And procedural obligations, formally guaranteeing older persons the right to access environmental information, public participation, and access to justice. Older persons must not only be framed as victims of climate change, but as active agents of change whose voices and capabilities are legally protected. Thank you.
